On October 2, 2026, law firm Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman, LLC announced it was investigating potential claims on behalf of Jackson Financial stockholders.

title: Astrana's debt doubled to $1.05 billion as its reported earnings came under scrutiny
points: GlassHouse Research published a short-seller report challenging Astrana's accounting.
Its report said debt had doubled to $1.05 billion and described a $545 million loan tied to dividend income.
Astrana shares fell 8% to $34.76 in early trading.
body: Astrana Health is a US healthcare company listed on Nasdaq. It reported growth driven by acquisitions and presented investors with earnings figures that included adjustments beyond standard accounting measures. GlassHouse Research questioned whether those figures reflected the company's underlying business.

On September 17, 2026, GlassHouse Research published a short-seller report challenging Astrana's accounting. The firm disclosed a short position, meaning it stood to profit if Astrana's shares fell. It examined reserves, acquisition accounting, settlement estimates, receivables and adjusted earnings.

GlassHouse alleged that Astrana's profits depended on management estimates that could conceal weaker financial performance. Its report said debt had doubled to $1.05 billion and described a $545 million loan tied to dividend income. It also questioned whether dividends from APC covered the loan's interest.

The report raised concerns about related-party arrangements and accounting estimates used in acquisitions. GlassHouse argued that these practices helped support reported earnings despite weaker underlying economics. These were the short seller's allegations, not findings by a court or regulator.
Astrana shares fell 8% to $34.76 in early trading. These figures described share-price movements, not cash losses or debt repayments.

title: Software from Israel powered hundreds of fake trading sites
points: The report alleged that almost all of Airsoft's clients ran fraudulent investment platforms rather than legitimate brokerages.
According to the investigation, the software allowed hundreds of fake trading websites to operate and put targeted sites back online within minutes after regulatory warnings.
The report alleged that these platforms took around 950 million euros from victims worldwide, including tens of millions of euros in losses in Germany.
body: Airsoft Ltd. was an Israeli technology company that presented its product as an all-in-one online brokerage software.

On September 17, 2026, Der Spiegel published an investigation based on thousands of documents it obtained and shared with the European Investigative Collaborations network. The report alleged that almost all of Airsoft's clients ran fraudulent investment platforms rather than legitimate brokerages.

According to the investigation, the software allowed hundreds of fake trading websites to operate and put targeted sites back online within minutes after regulatory warnings. The report alleged that these platforms took around 950 million euros from victims worldwide, including tens of millions of euros in losses in Germany.

In June 2026, the Bamberg Regional Court in Germany convicted Shay Benhamou, a former chief executive of Airsoft. The court sentenced him to four years in prison for aiding and abetting fraud in four cases.

title: A surrogacy agency announced bankruptcy. A Florida court ordered $87,415 returned.
points: Six surrogates and the family of another told OCCRP reporters that monthly payments had stopped as early as November 2025.
The court ordered the defendants to return $87,415 to the couple.
That amount was a separate claim, not part of the $87,415 judgment.
body: World Center of Baby was an international surrogacy agency that advertised services in Ukraine, Albania, Georgia, Cyprus, and Mexico. It promised prospective parents help finding surrogates and arranging medical care, legal work, and payments. Its apparent main U.S. entity was World Center Group Corp., registered in Florida.

In February 2026, the agency emailed clients that it was declaring bankruptcy. Six surrogates and the family of another told OCCRP reporters that monthly payments had stopped as early as November 2025. OCCRP found no federal bankruptcy filing for World Center Group Corp. at the time of its investigation.

Reporters examined corporate records and spoke with people affected by the collapse. They found that individuals named in company documents appeared to be proxies who claimed little involvement. Limassol police in Cyprus confirmed an investigation into allegations involving illegal surrogacy advertising.

A U.K.-based couple sued World Center Group Corp. and two representatives over payments for a surrogacy program. Florida Judge Thomas Ramsberger entered a default judgment after the defendants failed to respond to summons. The court ordered the defendants to return $87,415 to the couple.

OCCRP later reported that another intended parent had filed a separate lawsuit alleging more than $40,000 paid for medical procedures in Mexico had not been refunded. That amount was a separate claim, not part of the $87,415 judgment. The second lawsuit included allegations of fraud and breach of contract.

title: SWVL projected $1 billion in annual revenue. It delivered $24.2 million.
points: The report noted SWVL reported FY2025 revenue of $24.2 million, or 2.4% of its original target.
Fugazi Research cited an independent review of 135 recent Google Play reviews of the SWVL consumer app, finding 97.8% were negative.
It also noted SWVL raised approximately $14.5 million through two private placements, issuing about 10 million new shares at roughly $1.45 per share.
body: Swvl Holdings Corp is a transportation company that went public through Queen's Gambit Growth Capital, a SPAC, at a $1.5 billion valuation. It told investors it would expand into 20 countries and reach more than $1 billion in annual gross revenue by 2025. Before the deal closed, investors redeemed 84.6% of the SPAC trust, leaving $53.3 million in proceeds.

On September 11, 2026, short seller Fugazi Research published a report on the company. The report noted SWVL reported FY2025 revenue of $24.2 million, or 2.4% of its original target. Fugazi Research also alleged SWVL claimed its first profitable year twice, noting an earlier FY2023 profit of $3.06 million was 84% driven by $18.83 million in other income from creditor settlements at 15 cents on the dollar.

Fugazi Research cited an independent review of 135 recent Google Play reviews of the SWVL consumer app, finding 97.8% were negative. It also noted SWVL raised approximately $14.5 million through two private placements, issuing about 10 million new shares at roughly $1.45 per share.

Earlier, on August 25, 2026, shares rose over 50% from $1.49 to roughly $2.42 after SWVL announced a $13 million tranche led by Coefficient LP for a US expansion. By September 11, 2026, the stock had lost 90.4% of its public value to $143.7 million, an amount separate from annual revenue.

title: Two of TransAct's six board directors also sat on the board of a customer.
points: The firm stated it held exposure to TransAct shares, which it valued higher than the market's 0.7x enterprise value to sales multiple.
TransAct's proxy statements disclosed sales of food service technology products to ONE Group Hospitality in 2024 and 2025.
The report also argued against selling only the casino business and estimated the split businesses could be worth $100 million to $134 million.
body: TransAct Technologies is a company that went public on August 22, 1996, and sells casino and food service technology products. Thirty years later, its shares traded at about $5, below levels reached in the late 1990s.

On September 10, 2026, Ragnarok Research published a report examining the company's board and strategic plans. The firm stated it held exposure to TransAct shares, which it valued higher than the market's 0.7x enterprise value to sales multiple.

The report noted that two of TransAct's six directors, Emanuel Hilario and board chair Haydee Ortiz Olinger, also served on the board of ONE Group Hospitality. TransAct's proxy statements disclosed sales of food service technology products to ONE Group Hospitality in 2024 and 2025.

Ragnarok Research noted that Hilario chaired the audit committee, which oversaw the company's related party transactions policy, while Olinger owned 0.3% of TransAct's shares. The report also argued against selling only the casino business and estimated the split businesses could be worth $100 million to $134 million.

investigator: The Equity Dispatch, J Capital Research
title: Karman guided to $218.8 million in adjusted EBITDA without positive cash flow
points: J Capital alleged that Karman failed to generate positive operating cash flow while paying large sums for acquisitions repeatedly disclosed as not material.
It also alleged that Karman's guided adjusted EBITDA included a negative cash drag from rapidly building contract assets, and cited ongoing weak internal controls.
By late Friday night on September 4, 2026, Karman's shares were down 11% week to date.
body: Karman Holdings is a defense and space components maker listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It grew revenue by buying defense contractors and subcontractors with debt, and guided to about $218.8 million in adjusted EBITDA for 2026.
On September 2, 2026, short seller J Capital Research published a report on its Substack publication The Equity Dispatch. A short seller earns money when a company's shares fall.

J Capital alleged that Karman failed to generate positive operating cash flow while paying large sums for acquisitions repeatedly disclosed as not material. It also alleged that Karman's guided adjusted EBITDA included a negative cash drag from rapidly building contract assets, and cited ongoing weak internal controls.
By late Friday night on September 4, 2026, Karman's shares were down 11% week to date. As of September 4, 2026, the company had not formally responded to the report.

title: ZeroStack paid $163.4 million for 0G tokens. By June 2026, they were worth $15.2 million.
points: Fugazi Research cited company filings showing ZeroStack held 75,101,767 0G tokens as of June 30, 2026.
For the first six months of 2026, ZeroStack reported $20.9 million in revenue, a $61.3 million net loss, and $2.6 million in cash.
The report also noted that ZeroStack had completed two reverse stock splits, a 20-to-1 split in June 2023 and a 39-to-1 split in August 2025, reducing the share count by 780 to 1.
body: ZeroStack Corp is a Nasdaq-listed company that told investors it was a decentralized artificial intelligence treasury built around the 0G token. Before changing its name, the company operated as Flora Growth Corp and sold cannabis.

On August 31, 2026, short seller Fugazi Research published a report on ZeroStack. The report said ZeroStack was Flora Growth under a new ticker, with no meaningful change to its underlying pharmaceutical distribution business.

Fugazi Research cited company filings showing ZeroStack held 75,101,767 0G tokens as of June 30, 2026. The company paid a cost basis of $163.4 million for those tokens, which had fallen about 91% to a fair value of $15.2 million. For the first six months of 2026, ZeroStack reported $20.9 million in revenue, a $61.3 million net loss, and $2.6 million in cash.

The report also noted that ZeroStack had completed two reverse stock splits, a 20-to-1 split in June 2023 and a 39-to-1 split in August 2025, reducing the share count by 780 to 1. In a separate filing, ZeroStack registered over 54.6 million common shares for sale by existing stockholders and a shelf offering of up to $1 billion in securities.

title: DFDV traded at $5.28 a share against $215 million in liabilities
points: Shortfinder said the company carried $215 million in liabilities while holding only $4.3 million in cash and an unused $199 million at-the-market equity offering facility.
The report alleged that the SOL treasury was insufficient to cover the $215 million in liabilities.
The $215 million in liabilities is debt owed by the company, while the $3 per share figure is Shortfinder's estimate of overvaluation.
body: DeFi Development Corp., listed on Nasdaq under the ticker DFDV, is a publicly traded company whose main asset is a treasury of about 2.33 million SOL tokens. It used that token treasury as the basis for a stock price rally.

On August 28, 2026, short seller Shortfinder published a report on the company. Shortfinder said the company carried $215 million in liabilities while holding only $4.3 million in cash and an unused $199 million at-the-market equity offering facility.

The report alleged that the SOL treasury was insufficient to cover the $215 million in liabilities. Shortfinder alleged that stripping out the debt left intrinsic equity value at roughly $1.54 per share, compared with a market price of $5.28, making the stock overvalued by about $3 per share.
The $215 million in liabilities is debt owed by the company, while the $3 per share figure is Shortfinder's estimate of overvaluation. DFDV shares fell 58.94% since the report.

title: A nine-employee firm rose 350%, fell 92%, and bought a business with no orders
points: The shares rose about 350% in ten sessions to $12.25 on August 12, then fell about 92% in six sessions to an intraday $0.75 on August 20.
Zenta Group had filed a Form 6-K on August 7 stating it knew of no undisclosed material information.
Starting on August 26, 2026, Black Stone Insights published reports reviewing Zenta Group's public SEC filings and market data.
body: Zenta Group Company Limited is a Cayman Islands holding company for a nine-employee Macau consulting and financial-technology business. It listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market on September 9, 2025 at $4.00 per share and reported about $1.0 million in net income.

In August 2026, the shares rose about 350% in ten sessions to $12.25 on August 12, then fell about 92% in six sessions to an intraday $0.75 on August 20. Zenta Group had filed a Form 6-K on August 7 stating it knew of no undisclosed material information.

Starting on August 26, 2026, Black Stone Insights published reports reviewing Zenta Group's public SEC filings and market data. The reports highlighted the stock swing, a single principal supplier, four customers, and a ticker change from ZGM to ZTG in April 2026, while stating they did not allege fraud.

On September 25, 2026, Black Stone Insights noted that Zenta Group had closed a share-funded acquisition of ZentoAI worth up to $7.13 million, then disclosed 13 days later that the acquired business had no confirmed customer orders and no contracted revenue. The $7.13 million consideration and the 92% drop in share price are different amounts: one is the acquisition price, the other is the fall in market value.

title: Doctored photos and fake records cost an energy firm its accreditation
points: ABC News reported that Victorian authorities accused the company of fraud within the energy efficiency scheme.
The allegations stated that the firm falsified customer records and used doctored photographs to claim the government-backed certificates.
Following the fraud allegations, the state's Essential Services Commission stepped in and took regulatory action against the business.
body: Royal One Pty Ltd is an energy efficiency firm in Victoria, Australia. It participated in the state's Victorian Energy Upgrades program, which provides government-backed certificates to businesses.

On August 25, 2026, ABC News reported that Victorian authorities accused the company of fraud within the energy efficiency scheme. The allegations stated that the firm falsified customer records and used doctored photographs to claim the government-backed certificates.
Following the fraud allegations, the state's Essential Services Commission stepped in and took regulatory action against the business.
On August 25, 2026, the Essential Services Commission announced that it had suspended Royal One Pty Ltd's accreditation for the Victorian Energy Upgrades program.

title: Aeva carried a $1.3 billion market value on $18.1 million in sales
points: It said Aeva's $1.3 billion market value equaled 72 times its 2025 revenue of $18.1 million, while net losses totaled $447 million over three years.
The report alleged Aeva relied on high-profile partner announcements and share sales rather than commercial deliveries.
A Goldman Sachs analyst issued a $20.00 price target for the stock, which was then trading at $18.29.
body: Aeva Technologies is a Nasdaq-listed developer of lidar sensors. The company told investors it was launching optical connectivity for AI data centers alongside a joint development agreement.

On August 21, 2026, short seller Fugazi Research reviewed Aeva's SEC filings and published a report. It said Aeva's $1.3 billion market value equaled 72 times its 2025 revenue of $18.1 million, while net losses totaled $447 million over three years.

The report alleged Aeva relied on high-profile partner announcements and share sales rather than commercial deliveries. It noted that first-half 2026 revenue was $12.4 million against a net loss of $114.6 million, and that initial hyperscaler deployment was targeted for the second half of 2027.
Aeva's shares fell the morning the report came out. On August 24, 2026, a Goldman Sachs analyst issued a $20.00 price target for the stock, which was then trading at $18.29.

title: Guggenheim fund paid $1.74 billion in dividends while issuing shares above asset value
points: The report alleged that the fund paid $1.74 billion over eight fiscal years by issuing common shares above net asset value 125 times in a row from March 2016 through July 2026.
It also said the fund held twin $20 million notes from Canadian shell companies and $23 million from a 12-week-old U.K. shell company.
Shares fell $0.67, or 6.64%, to close at $9.42 on August 20, 2026.
body: Guggenheim Strategic Opportunities Fund is a closed-end leveraged multisector credit fund listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It pays investors $0.18 a share per month, or over 20% a year on net asset value.

On August 20, 2026, The Bear Cave published a report after reviewing 19 years of the fund's audited financials and SEC filings. Hunterbrook Capital, affiliated with the newsletter's publisher, held a short position in the shares.

The report alleged that the fund paid $1.74 billion over eight fiscal years by issuing common shares above net asset value 125 times in a row from March 2016 through July 2026. It also said the fund held twin $20 million notes from Canadian shell companies and $23 million from a 12-week-old U.K. shell company.
Shares fell $0.67, or 6.64%, to close at $9.42 on August 20, 2026. A fund spokesperson pointed to its 19-year track record and Morningstar 5-Star rating.
On August 31, 2026, law firm Kaplan Fox & Kilsheimer LLP announced it was investigating potential securities law violations involving the fund.

title: Twist Bioscience reached $200 a share before two short sellers questioned its value
points: Twist Bioscience shares rose 22.64% to $142.39 on August 19, 2026, and later climbed to around $200 a share during a short squeeze.
Scorpion Capital flagged a $56.3 million stock sale by the chief executive under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan.
The report argued that market optimism had detached from the core business economics, and Twist Bioscience shares fell 10% that day.
body: Twist Bioscience is a synthetic biology company listed on Nasdaq. Its shares surged after Anthropic named it an independent evaluator in an AI-driven protein design campaign, and its chief executive struck a bullish tone on earnings.

On August 19, 2026, short seller Scorpion Capital posted a report on X and disclosed a short position, which earns when shares fall. It called the company a cash-burning inferno operating a Ponzi-like scheme and labeled its AI narrative a speculative delusion.

Twist Bioscience shares rose 22.64% to $142.39 on August 19, 2026, and later climbed to around $200 a share during a short squeeze. Scorpion Capital flagged a $56.3 million stock sale by the chief executive under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan.

On November 5, 2026, The Bear Cave published a report by Hunterbrook Media's chief executive after interviewing Twist Bioscience's chief executive. The report argued that market optimism had detached from the core business economics, and Twist Bioscience shares fell 10% that day.

title: Flock said its cameras could not track people. Its own website held 450 AI files.
points: WIRED published an investigation after finding a cache of more than 450 files on Flock's own website, served by its login pages.
WIRED reconstructed the software and said the artificial intelligence tool could identify drivers and track vehicles by their movement patterns alone.
WIRED and 404 Media reported they had analyzed data hackers copied from a Flock camera across 27,321 video clips, finding no face-recognition capabilities beyond Android defaults.
body: Flock Safety is a United States vehicle surveillance company that sells license plate cameras to police. For years, the company told the public that its technology could not recognize, identify, or track individuals.

On August 19, 2026, WIRED published an investigation after finding a cache of more than 450 files on Flock's own website, served by its login pages. WIRED reconstructed the software and said the artificial intelligence tool could identify drivers and track vehicles by their movement patterns alone.

In Alpharetta, Georgia, WIRED found through public records requests that Flock camera data was accessible to more than 2,000 agencies, while the city received data from more than 1,300 entities. On September 16, 2026, WIRED and 404 Media reported they had analyzed data hackers copied from a Flock camera across 27,321 video clips, finding no face-recognition capabilities beyond Android defaults.

Flock did not respond to most of WIRED's detailed questions on its hardware supply chain, though it contested a proposed OSHA penalty of about $9,500, saying it had reported a workplace injury quickly.

title: Flotek touted a $400 million Puerto Rico deal. Wolfpack said it was already canceled.
points: Wolfpack cited court filings, a synopsis from a financial regulator, and accusations of an unauthorized signature that became publicly known on August 7.
Flotek's shares dropped 20% on August 17, 2026, the company's worst day in over six years.
The drop in share price and the $400 million contract value are separate amounts: the first is a stock market decline, while the second is the stated size of the alleged canceled deal.
body: Flotek Industries is a New York Stock Exchange-listed company. It had announced a $400 million power deal in Puerto Rico involving the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority and Power Expectations, and discussed the contract with investors.

On August 17, 2026, short seller Wolfpack Research published a report alleging that the $400 million contract had been canceled. Wolfpack said it held a short position in Flotek's securities, meaning it earns when the shares fall.

Wolfpack cited court filings, a synopsis from a financial regulator, and accusations of an unauthorized signature that became publicly known on August 7. According to Wolfpack's analysis, the deal accounted for 57% of Flotek's backlog from 2027 to 2030, and Flotek had failed to disclose the cancellation to investors.

Flotek's shares dropped 20% on August 17, 2026, the company's worst day in over six years. The drop in share price and the $400 million contract value are separate amounts: the first is a stock market decline, while the second is the stated size of the alleged canceled deal.

investigator: The Capitol Forum, The Capital Forum
title: VITAS collected $4,000 more per hospice patient than the national average.
points: In later reports through November 3, 2026, it alleged VITAS misdiagnosed dementia patients and falsified evaluation scores.
An analysis of 2024 Medicare claims data found Medicare paid VITAS roughly 26%, or $4,000, more per patient than the national average.
Chemed had previously paid $75 million and entered a five-year corporate integrity agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services over similar false Medicare claims.
body: VITAS Healthcare is a subsidiary of Chemed and the largest hospice provider in the United States. The company provides end-of-life care and bills Medicare for its services.

On August 13, 2026, The Capitol Forum reported that VITAS may have systematically overbilled Medicare by tens of millions of dollars annually for continuous home care. In later reports through November 3, 2026, it alleged VITAS misdiagnosed dementia patients and falsified evaluation scores.

The Capitol Forum also alleged that VITAS enrolled actively dying hospital patients to skirt Medicare payment caps, and in some cases billed for deceased patients. An analysis of 2024 Medicare claims data found Medicare paid VITAS roughly 26%, or $4,000, more per patient than the national average.
Chemed had previously paid $75 million and entered a five-year corporate integrity agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services over similar false Medicare claims.
In August 2026, Georgia regulators placed VITAS's state operations under immediate jeopardy after finding dying patients waited hours for a nurse and a full day for medications.

title: Blue Moon said it was fully financed. Its $140 million loan had no final agreements.
points: Viceroy Research, which held a short position and stood to gain if the share price fell, published reports starting August 13, 2026.
Kargl-Simard dismissed Viceroy's work during a call with brokers on August 13, 2026.
Blue Moon announced that its acquisition of 33 tungsten and antimony projects in the western United States was dead.
body: Blue Moon Metals is a mining company listed on the TSX Venture Exchange. On August 11, 2026, chief executive Christian Kargl-Simard said the company was fully financed to build all four of its mines, including its Norwegian flagship project Nussir.

Viceroy Research, which held a short position and stood to gain if the share price fell, published reports starting August 13, 2026. The investigator said Blue Moon raised C$156.25 million in May 2026 after telling investors Nussir would be funded partly by a US$140 million project finance package, when final agreements for the US$50 million term loan and US$70 million stream were never signed.

Kargl-Simard dismissed Viceroy's work during a call with brokers on August 13, 2026. On September 25, 2026, Norway delegated authority to its Ministry of Climate and Environment to reverse sea-disposal approvals from a 2016 royal decree while examining whether Nussir's permit had the same defect.

On November 2, 2026, Blue Moon announced that its acquisition of 33 tungsten and antimony projects in the western United States was dead. The next day, the company announced it was selling Blue Moon Norway and Nussir to ACG Metals for $220 million in ACG shares.

title: The Army paid $533 million for an artillery factory. It made zero usable shells.
points: The factory opened in May 2024, and robots inside caught fire while equipment repeatedly failed.
ProPublica reported that the plant did not produce a single usable shell and missed eight deadlines, leading the Army to halt two of its three production lines in August 2025.
Since the Army halted the two lines, the General Dynamics unit received $2.5 billion in new contract awards.
body: General Dynamics is a United States defense contractor. Starting in November 2022, the U.S. Army paid the company $533 million in no-bid awards to build a new factory in Mesquite, Texas, to make 155 mm artillery shell bodies.

On August 12, 2026, ProPublica published an investigation based on internal company documents, photos, video, and interviews with 36 current and former workers and officials. ProPublica reported that General Dynamics used equipment from a Turkish subcontractor, Repkon, without inspecting full production lines in action first.

The factory opened in May 2024, and robots inside caught fire while equipment repeatedly failed. ProPublica reported that the plant did not produce a single usable shell and missed eight deadlines, leading the Army to halt two of its three production lines in August 2025.

General Dynamics declined an interview and said ProPublica fundamentally mischaracterized the circumstances, though it did not specify any errors. The company also told a Department of Defense inspector general that it met or exceeded requirements.

In a statement to ProPublica, the Army said it was evaluating contract performance and would recover funds through unspecified discounts on production orders. Since the Army halted the two lines, the General Dynamics unit received $2.5 billion in new contract awards.

title: Curaleaf said its shareholders owed nothing. Records showed a $25.4 million debt.
points: Federal grand juries and the FBI examined Curaleaf's financing and shareholders in money laundering and public corruption probes starting in October 2018.
According to the report, Abramovich's offshore companies lent $85 million to Curaleaf in August 2018 and injected $120 million in 2020 and 2021.
Curaleaf said it was never notified that it was a subject of any FBI investigation and complied with ownership disclosure rules.
body: Curaleaf Holdings is a cannabis company that went public on the Canadian Securities Exchange on October 29, 2018. In a public statement, Curaleaf said it and its primary shareholders did not owe outstanding funds to Russian businessman Roman Abramovich.

On August 11, 2026, The Newsground published FBI records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request alongside leaked corporate records. Federal grand juries and the FBI examined Curaleaf's financing and shareholders in money laundering and public corruption probes starting in October 2018.

According to the report, Abramovich's offshore companies lent $85 million to Curaleaf in August 2018 and injected $120 million in 2020 and 2021. Corporate records reviewed by The Newsground also showed that chairman Boris Jordan's company Gociter Holdings owed Abramovich's Cetus Investments $25.4 million, which remained unpaid at the end of 2023.

Curaleaf said it was never notified that it was a subject of any FBI investigation and complied with ownership disclosure rules. No charges resulted from the probes described in the released records. On September 7, 2026, The Newsground revised its first headline after correspondence with lawyers for Curaleaf and Jordan.

points: The report alleged that ZenaTech CEO Shaun Passley caused ZENA to advance approximately C$28.2 million in cash to his separately controlled company Epazz for research and development.

body: ZenaTech is a software technology company specializing in drones that is listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol ZENA.

On August 10, 2026, short seller White Diamond Research published a report stating it held a short position and stood to gain if the stock fell. The report alleged that ZenaTech CEO Shaun Passley caused ZENA to advance approximately C$28.2 million in cash to his separately controlled company Epazz for research and development.

title: Netcapital booked $13.9 million from startups paying in their own shares
points: Short seller Fugazi Research summarized the filing in reports published on November 17, 2026.
The SEC alleged that Netcapital recognized approximately $13.9 million in improper revenue, inflating reported figures by about 345%.
Its fiscal 2026 annual report and Q1 fiscal 2027 report were delinquent, and Nasdaq granted an extension until February 9, 2027.
body: Netcapital Inc. is a crowdfunding platform listed on Nasdaq. Between October 2021 and January 2024, it reported $17.95 million in total revenue across ten quarters.

On August 10, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission filed a civil complaint against Netcapital and five individuals. Short seller Fugazi Research summarized the filing in reports published on November 17, 2026.

The SEC alleged that Netcapital recognized approximately $13.9 million in improper revenue, inflating reported figures by about 345%. At least eleven startups controlled by John Fanning signed consulting deals worth $1 million to $2 million each and paid in their own equity. Comparable legitimate customers paid about $50,000.

On August 12, 2026, independent auditor Fruci & Associates II resigned, citing the SEC action. Netcapital later told investors not to rely on its audited financial statements for fiscal 2022 through 2025.

Netcapital engaged a successor auditor to re-audit those years and fiscal 2026. By November 2026, its fiscal 2026 annual report and Q1 fiscal 2027 report were delinquent, and Nasdaq granted an extension until February 9, 2027.

title: Vineland halted work at Nebius's 300-megawatt site. Executives still called it on track.
points: On August 13 and August 14, 2026, investigative organization Hunterbrook Media reported that it had reviewed municipal documents and contacted Vineland officials.
Hunterbrook reported that the City of Vineland had issued two stop-construction orders over unpermitted work on the site's power infrastructure.
Nebius did not respond, while a DataOne spokesperson said the company did not expect the temporary pause to affect its construction and delivery timeline.
body: Nebius Group N.V. is a company developing a roughly 300-megawatt data center in Vineland, whose capacity Microsoft has contracted to use. On its second-quarter earnings call, Nebius told investors the Vineland project was on track.

On August 13 and August 14, 2026, investigative organization Hunterbrook Media reported that it had reviewed municipal documents and contacted Vineland officials. Hunterbrook reported that the City of Vineland had issued two stop-construction orders over unpermitted work on the site's power infrastructure.

DataOne was installing Bloom Energy fuel cells and a liquefied natural gas tank without prior approval or permits. Hunterbrook's affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, held a short position in Bloom Energy at the time of publication.

According to Hunterbrook, Nebius executives did not mention the stop-construction orders when asked about the Vineland project on the earnings call two days after the second order. Nebius did not respond, while a DataOne spokesperson said the company did not expect the temporary pause to affect its construction and delivery timeline.
Vineland officials had ordered the unpermitted installation work halted, and the city's building code office told Hunterbrook it was instructed not to discuss the issue.

title: LaSalle Corrections told the public it was one company. Its lawyers called it a trade name.
points: Hunterbrook Media published a monthslong investigation into the company and reviewed a decade of litigation.
Hunterbrook alleged that the family behind LaSalle built a liability moat using nearly 80 limited liability companies.

body: LaSalle Corrections is a family-operated private prison company headquartered in Louisiana. It presents itself to the public as a single prison enterprise.

On August 6, 2026, Hunterbrook Media published a monthslong investigation into the company and reviewed a decade of litigation. Its investment affiliate, Hunterbrook Capital, held no positions related to the article at publication.

Hunterbrook alleged that the family behind LaSalle built a liability moat using nearly 80 limited liability companies. When families sue over inmate deaths, LaSalle lawyers argue that LaSalle Corrections is only a trade name for separate local companies, trapping claims inside the entities that run each facility.

In one lawsuit, LaSalle moved to dismiss a claim because the plaintiff failed to name LaSalle Corrections West, the entity holding the jail contract. In another lawsuit, the Anderson legal team admitted that naming LaSalle Corrections LLC as a defendant was a mistake.

title: Block's shares fell 22% after a report questioned Cash App's user numbers
points: Hindenburg Research spent two years investigating Block and took a short position, which would profit if the shares fell.

Block's shares fell as much as 22% after the report appeared, then recovered partly to trade down 15%.
body: Block Inc. is a US payments company led by Jack Dorsey. Its Cash App serves customers, including people without bank accounts. Block reported its transacting user base as a key measure of the app's performance.

Hindenburg Research spent two years investigating Block and took a short position, which would profit if the shares fell. Its researchers interviewed multiple former employees who said internal concerns were suppressed and user complaints were ignored. Hindenburg alleged that weak compliance controls allowed fraud and criminal activity on Cash App.

The report also alleged that Block inflated its user numbers and understated customer acquisition costs. Hindenburg claimed that up to 35% of Cash App's revenue came from interchange fees, representing around $892 million in revenue that it said should face legal caps. That figure concerned revenue, not a proven loss.

Block's shares fell as much as 22% after the report appeared, then recovered partly to trade down 15%. Block called the report factually inaccurate and misleading, said it was exploring legal action against Hindenburg, and said it would work with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

title: REalloys reported $706,000 in revenue and $81.8 million in stock pay

title: Lyft had $533 million in legal and tax accruals against up to $2.7 billion in claims
points: The firm reviewed court dockets and spoke with two former Lyft employees and multiple insurance executives.
The exposure estimate and the cash balance are different amounts: the first is an alleged legal liability, and the second is money on the balance sheet.
A Lyft spokesperson said the report was the opinion of one short-selling firm and inaccurately suggested that the claims fell outside Lyft's insurance coverage.
body: Lyft is a ride-hailing company that holds about 24% of the U.S. market. In its FY2025 10-K and Q1 2026 10-Q filings, the company did not disclose that sexual assault cases against it were consolidated into Multi-District Litigation, and it did not list a specific sexual assault accrual on its balance sheet.

On July 23, 2026, Bleecker Street Research published a report and disclosed that funds it manages held a short position in Lyft, meaning it earns when the shares fall. The firm reviewed court dockets and spoke with two former Lyft employees and multiple insurance executives.

The report alleged that Lyft faced an estimated $1.3 billion to $2.7 billion in exposure from 56 Multi-District Litigation cases, 2,000 California state court cases, and at least 700 unfiled cases. It said Lyft held only $533 million in combined legal and tax accruals and $1.7 billion in unrestricted cash and investments, while its $2.3 billion in insurance reserves were for commercial auto claims.

The exposure estimate and the cash balance are different amounts: the first is an alleged legal liability, and the second is money on the balance sheet. By July 27, 2026, a Lyft spokesperson said the report was the opinion of one short-selling firm and inaccurately suggested that the claims fell outside Lyft's insurance coverage.

title: Two insurers loaned about $21 billion to Mark Walter's conduits

body: Delaware Life Insurance Company is a US insurer providing annuities and life insurance, serving customers in Massachusetts and Kansas.

On November 12, 2026, Bloomberg News reported that an analysis of over 400 Delaware records showed Delaware Life and Clear Spring Life and Annuity loaned about $21 billion to apparent Mark Walter financial conduits. Federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission opened investigations into how the insurers invested billions in Walter's businesses without required regulatory disclosures. Delaware Life and Clear Spring received grand jury subpoenas in February.

In August 2026, Walter's holding company TWG Global agreed to buy up to $6.5 billion of affiliated assets from Delaware Life, while banks paused sales of its products. On November 17, 2026, a filing showed third-quarter premiums and annuity considerations fell 33% from the previous period to $1.8 billion.

title: Phia claimed commissions on shopping sales its browser tool did not drive
points: Bloomberg News reported that Phia's browser extension claimed credit for purchases even when shoppers never used it.
On July 8, Phia said it had learned of the situation only within the previous 24 hours.
On August 11, Bloomberg published its findings about the founders' involvement.
body: Phia is a US advertising startup co-founded by Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni. It calls its browser tool a personal shopping assistant that finds lower prices and discount codes for clothes and accessories. Retailers pay Phia commissions when the tool helps shoppers buy products.

On July 9, 2026, Bloomberg News reported that Phia's browser extension claimed credit for purchases even when shoppers never used it. The practice increased commissions paid to Phia for sales it had not helped generate.

Bloomberg reviewed historical source code and confirmed the features existed. Internal Slack messages and people familiar with the matter indicated that both founders pushed for the features and knew about the practice for at least seven months, going back to December.

The practice involved purchases from retailers including Nike, Gap and Nordstrom, and was broadly prohibited by Phia's commercial partners. On July 8, Phia said it had learned of the situation only within the previous 24 hours.
On August 11, Bloomberg published its findings about the founders' involvement. Two people familiar with the matter said the internal exchanges were no longer visible to Phia employees.

title: Soft2Bet ran 11 licensed betting brands and received €600 million from shadow casinos
points: Reporters found 145 blacklisted websites connected to the group, and a Star reporter opened an account at unlicensed site OnlySpins.com without age verification.
Soft2Bet denied wrongdoing and said the reporting reflected an incorrect and misleading interpretation of its corporate structure.
Ontario's gambling regulator said it was reviewing the allegations regarding ToonieBet and Soft2Bet.
body: Soft2Bet is a Malta-based gambling company that operates licensed online betting sites, including ToonieBet in Ontario, and says it operates responsibly according to regulations. Publicly, the business consists of 11 betting brands and software sales.

On July 8, 2026, Investigate Europe and the Toronto Star published an investigation with media partners across 15 countries. Reporters reviewed thousands of pages of leaked payment statements, internal chat screenshots, corporate records, and interviewed six former employees.

The investigation alleged that between 2020 and 2024, Soft2Bet and its partners received €600 million, or nearly $1 billion, via shell companies and payment agents from offshore casinos blacklisted in Europe. Reporters found 145 blacklisted websites connected to the group, and a Star reporter opened an account at unlicensed site OnlySpins.com without age verification.
Soft2Bet denied wrongdoing and said the reporting reflected an incorrect and misleading interpretation of its corporate structure.

On July 10, 2026, Ontario's gambling regulator said it was reviewing the allegations regarding ToonieBet and Soft2Bet. By July 27, 2026, OnlySpins shut down, another linked site named Betwarts announced it would close on July 31, and regulators in Ireland launched a probe into more than 100 websites linked to Soft2Bet.

body: Bloom Energy sells fuel cells to power data centers and reached a market value around $100 billion. The company told investors it did not rely on China for scandium, a rare earth element used in its fuel cells.

In July 2026, Hunterbrook reported that it held a short position in the stock and had examined global trade data, corporate filings, and shipping records. Hunterbrook said it traced over 154 metric tons of ceramic electrolyte membranes from China's Three Circle Group unit Glory Winner through Thailand between July 2024 and November 2025, marked BE PALLET.

In further reports on July 30 and August 6, 2026, Hunterbrook analyzed public data from 126 U.S. plants and South Korean sites. The report alleged that all 37 New York systems fell below Bloom's efficiency benchmark at a median of 20 months, and that 74% of fourth-quarter 2025 revenue, or $574 million of $778 million, came from joint ventures Bloom part-owned with Brookfield.

Bloom filed a Form 8-K with the SEC rejecting Hunterbrook's financial and accounting claims, and denied relying on Chinese scandium in a blog post and on an earnings call. On November 10, 2026, Hunterbrook reported that shipments of ceramic electrolyte membranes from Thailand marked BE PALLET had resumed arriving in Oakland in September 2026 after a hiatus of more than nine months.

body: Ubiquiti is a $33 billion US technology company that makes wireless networking equipment, including radio bridge antennae. Its chief executive, Robert Pera, had pledged to tighten controls on the company's products years earlier.

On June 26, 2026, investigative outlet Hunterbrook published a report alleging that Ubiquiti equipment served a critical communications role for Russian forces in Ukraine. Its affiliate, Hunterbrook Capital, held a short position in Ubiquiti shares, earning money if the stock fell.

points: Without those changes, fee-related earnings would have fallen 16%.

It stated that more than 70% of secondary returns did not come from day-one markups and said it was exploring legal and regulatory recourse.
body: Hamilton Lane is a Conshohocken, Pennsylvania investment firm that manages private market funds, including the roughly $6 billion Hamilton Lane Private Assets Fund. It told investors that its fee-related earnings grew 37% over the last nine months of 2025.

On June 26, 2026, Hunterbrook published a report alleging that about one-third of the fund's valuation gains came from immediate accounting markups when buying discounted stakes, rather than company growth. Hunterbrook's affiliated fund held a short position in Hamilton Lane shares.

Hunterbrook also alleged that Hamilton Lane changed its fee rules to collect performance fees on unrealized gains and exclude stock-based compensation, taking $58 million in incentive fees in the year ended March 2025. Without those changes, fee-related earnings would have fallen 16%.

Hamilton Lane shares fell on the afternoon of the report, and the firm pushed back against the allegations. It stated that more than 70% of secondary returns did not come from day-one markups and said it was exploring legal and regulatory recourse.

title: SpaceX had bought no Velo3D printers since 2022. The stock fell 9%.
points: The firm held short positions in Velo3D, meaning it stood to gain if the shares fell.
Morpheus alleged that SpaceX had bought no new Velo3D printer since 2022.
Former employees said Velo3D licensed its intellectual property to SpaceX in October 2024, allowing SpaceX to build its own machines.
body: Velo3D is a California company that makes industrial 3D printers. SpaceX was an early major customer, and Velo3D promoted that relationship as part of its shift toward aerospace and defense. Under CEO Arun Jeldi, its market value reached $537 million.

On June 25, 2026, Morpheus Research published a report based on 16 interviews with industry experts, former employees and customers. The firm held short positions in Velo3D, meaning it stood to gain if the shares fell.

Morpheus alleged that SpaceX had bought no new Velo3D printer since 2022. Former employees said Velo3D licensed its intellectual property to SpaceX in October 2024, allowing SpaceX to build its own machines. Morpheus also questioned the company's defense deals and claims about Jeldi's business background.
The report challenged Jeldi's December 2025 claim that SpaceX was expanding its printer fleet and buying printed parts from Velo3D. Shares fell 9% to $16.39 near midday on June 25.
On October 6, 2026, Morpheus Research still listed its Velo3D report, alleging that Jeldi had turned a failed SPAC and the disputed SpaceX relationship into a $390 million fortune.

investigator: J Capital Research, The Equity Dispatch
title: Data centers made up 7% of Microchip's business. Its shares were up 46%.
points: It said data center sales were reported at $302.7 million, or about 7% of the business, and that Data Center and Compute revenue had declined over the past four years.
It also said competitors Broadcom and Marvell recorded data center sales of $20 billion and $4 billion in 2025.
Microchip shares fell 2.8% on the day of the J Capital Research report.
body: Microchip Technology Incorporated is a US semiconductor company listed on Nasdaq. Its shares rose 46% from the start of 2026 on AI enthusiasm and a claimed recovery from customer overstocking, reaching an all-time high on May 7, 2026.

On June 24, 2026, short seller J Capital Research published a report on the company. It said data center sales were reported at $302.7 million, or about 7% of the business, and that Data Center and Compute revenue had declined over the past four years.

J Capital Research said Microchip had the lowest ratio of capital spending to depreciation among nine competitors and lacked the equipment to support its expected 67% data center growth. It also said competitors Broadcom and Marvell recorded data center sales of $20 billion and $4 billion in 2025.
Microchip shares fell 2.8% on the day of the J Capital Research report.
On October 9, 2026, short seller A Peek Behind the Numbers noted that Microchip's shares jumped nearly 14% after its Q1'27 earnings announcement reported strong growth and an upbeat outlook.

title: EquipmentShare raised $77 million through undisclosed related parties
points: The report stated that most of the company branches hemorrhage money, and that revenues and costs were shuffled between branches.
Short seller Blue Orca Capital also published a report that it was short the stock, and the shares fell 6 percent that day.
The company sought to reassure the market that its financial statements are independently audited by a Big 4 accounting firm.
body: EquipmentShare rents heavy equipment such as forklifts and excavators, and told investors that its branch network was ramping to industry-leading margins.

On June 24, 2026, short seller Umibozu Research published a report saying that the company used undisclosed related-party transactions to net at least $77 million for entities affiliated with founders Jabbok and Willy Schlacks. On September 24, 2026, short seller Blue Orca Capital also published a report that it was short the stock, and the shares fell 6 percent that day. The company sought to reassure the market that its financial statements are independently audited by a Big 4 accounting firm.
The company raised full-year guidance and deflected investors to boilerplate related-party disclosures on its website.

title: Hyliion shares jumped 150% on a $133 million order from a new buyer
points: The firm alleged the $133 million letter of intent was misrepresented because VFG Holdings was incorporated in January 2026 and lacked the capacity to support an order of that size.
Pelican Way also said CEO Thomas Healy had paid himself more since 2021 than Hyliion generated in total revenue.
The shares had rallied 150% on the letter of intent before collapsing after the report challenged the deal.
body: Hyliion Holdings Corp is a US energy technology company listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It builds the KARNO linear generator and told investors its power modules could serve AI data centers, highlighting a letter of intent worth about $133 million from VFG Holdings for 250 units.

In June 2026, short seller Pelican Way Research published a report on Hyliion, standing to profit if the stock fell. The firm alleged the $133 million letter of intent was misrepresented because VFG Holdings was incorporated in January 2026 and lacked the capacity to support an order of that size. Pelican Way also said CEO Thomas Healy had paid himself more since 2021 than Hyliion generated in total revenue.

The shares had rallied 150% on the letter of intent before collapsing after the report challenged the deal. The $133 million order value and the stock drop are separate amounts: the first was a non-binding purchase figure, and the second was a fall in market price.

On August 11, 2026, Hyliion reported second-quarter earnings, and the stock spiked 26.3% after hours. The gain disappeared by the next trading session, leaving shares at $3.92, 53% below their June high.

title: FreeCast held $119,302 in cash while its shares reached $12.20
points: For the quarter ending March 31, 2026, FreeCast reported $92,909 in revenue and a loss of more than $4.5 million, with $119,302 in cash and over $10 million in cumulative losses.
The report alleged that the company's SEC filings flagged substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern.
The report stated the shares were fundamentally of zero value.
body: FreeCast, Inc. is listed on Nasdaq and announced an expanded DIRECTV partnership on June 11, 2026, and a Starlink Business reseller agreement on June 18, 2026. The stock doubled on June 18 as more than 100 million shares traded, climbing from about $0.64 to an intraday high of $12.20 over a few days.

On June 22, 2026, Fugazi Research published a report examining FreeCast's SEC filings. For the quarter ending March 31, 2026, FreeCast reported $92,909 in revenue and a loss of more than $4.5 million, with $119,302 in cash and over $10 million in cumulative losses.

The report alleged that the company's SEC filings flagged substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. It also alleged that Nextelligence, another company controlled by CEO Mobley, paid off debts owed to FreeCast by Celebrity Cigars and Test Drive Live and booked the payoff as a new loan FreeCast owed back to Nextelligence.

Fugazi Research noted that a $50 million equity line of credit became drawable on May 6, 2026, before the June announcements, and that most of 6.7 million repriced warrants expired unexercised weeks earlier. The report stated the shares were fundamentally of zero value.

title: Deep Fission promised $50 power. A report found costs up to $289.
points: Deep Fission denied the report's doubts about its viability.
Stockholder rights law firm Johnson Fistel announced an investigation into potential securities claims following the report.
News reports noted the stock had dropped 50% after the critical report.
body: Deep Fission is a California-based nuclear startup listed on Nasdaq that plans to bury small reactors one mile underground in boreholes. Before its June 2026 initial public offering, the company told investors its reactors would produce power at a levelized cost of $50 to $70 per megawatt-hour.

On September 24, 2026, short seller Iceberg Research published a report and disclosed it held a short position in the stock. Using figures from Deep Fission's own June 2026 prospectus, Iceberg calculated energy costs of $289 per megawatt-hour for the first reactor and $148 for later units, about 200% above prior guidance.

Iceberg also alleged that Deep Fission faced $350 million in unfunded capital needs and that only 4 gigawatts of its claimed 18.5-gigawatt customer pipeline tied to identifiable counterparties under non-binding deals. Deep Fission denied the report's doubts about its viability.

On October 5, 2026, stockholder rights law firm Johnson Fistel announced an investigation into potential securities claims following the report. By October 21, 2026, news reports noted the stock had dropped 50% after the critical report.

title: Polymarket put its offshore unit in Panama. Its staff worked in New York.
points: Chief executive Shayne Coplan, who is based in New York, replaced Diana Munoz as president of Adventure One QSS two months after its 2021 incorporation.
Separately, on June 22, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported on a Polymarket marketing campaign promoting fake bets on social media.
Polymarket said it was committed to maintaining accurate, fair, and transparent markets.
body: Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based betting platform where users wager on elections and other events. In 2022, federal regulators barred it from serving U.S. customers and fined an associated entity, Blockratize, $1.4 million.
To comply, Polymarket transferred operations for its flagship platform to Adventure One QSS, an entity registered in Panama. WIRED examined the structure and spoke with former employees.

WIRED reported that Adventure One QSS had staff residing in New York and working from Polymarket's Manhattan headquarters, while its Panama City office was empty. Chief executive Shayne Coplan, who is based in New York, replaced Diana Munoz as president of Adventure One QSS two months after its 2021 incorporation.

Separately, on June 22, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported on a Polymarket marketing campaign promoting fake bets on social media. Polymarket said it was committed to maintaining accurate, fair, and transparent markets.
On June 26, 2026, two U.S. senators asked the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to disclose whether it was investigating Polymarket's marketing practices.

title: Hercules booked $55.9 million in loan income while collecting $4.9 million in cash
points: Hunterbrook analyzed 16 quarters of earnings-call disclosures and filings.
It also said payment-in-kind loan income doubled in two years to $55.9 million in 2025, while cash collected on those loans fell 73% to $4.9 million.
The company denied the claims, stating that 63% of new fundings since 2022 went to new borrowers and that PwC audited its valuations.
body: Hercules Capital is a business development company that lends money to startups. It told investors its loan valuations followed a rigorous, board-approved process and that its software loans were worth 100 cents on the dollar.

On February 27, 2026, Hunterbrook Media published a report while its affiliate Hunterbrook Capital held a short position, earning when the shares fall. Hunterbrook analyzed 16 quarters of earnings-call disclosures and filings.

The report alleged that about 35% of the portfolio, or $1.5 billion, was software debt, while companies like Houzz and AppDirect were placed in other categories. It also said payment-in-kind loan income doubled in two years to $55.9 million in 2025, while cash collected on those loans fell 73% to $4.9 million.
Hercules shares fell 7.9%, or $1.22, to $14.21 that day. The company denied the claims, stating that 63% of new fundings since 2022 went to new borrowers and that PwC audited its valuations.
On April 27, 2026, law firm Levi & Korsinsky announced a shareholder class action lawsuit over the alleged valuation and software concentration gaps.

title: A $610 million contract went to a site created on the day of the announcement
points: Short seller Grizzly Research published a report alleging that almost the entire revenue of 2CRSi was fabricated through an undisclosed related-party scheme with Joseph Church.
The company suspended its trading on June 19, 2026, after its shares fell 43% that day following the accusations.
The shares fell another 30% despite the company's denial.
body: 2CRSi is a French technology group that designs, manufactures, and distributes high-performance servers and told investors it had secured substantial contracts, including a $610 million agreement and a $290 million purchase order.

On June 18, 2026, short seller Grizzly Research published a report alleging that almost the entire revenue of 2CRSi was fabricated through an undisclosed related-party scheme with Joseph Church. The investigator stated that the unnamed client behind the $610 million contract was Church's company NewYork GreenCloud, which was created on the day of the contract announcement by 2CRSi and whose website was created and hosted by 2CRSi's IT department.
The company suspended its trading on June 19, 2026, after its shares fell 43% that day following the accusations. 2CRSi denied the allegations.
On June 22, 2026, the shares fell another 30% despite the company's denial.

title: Rockpoint promised steady growth while its sales backlog fell 37%
points: DF Research reviewed Rockpoint's financial filings and the history of its core assets, which were previously public as Niska Gas Storage before collapsing.
The report alleged that Rockpoint is a cyclical business dependent on natural gas spreads rather than a stable growth company.
Rockpoint's shares shrugged off the report and finished higher.
body: Rockpoint Gas Storage Inc. is a Canadian company listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange and is North America's largest independent pure-play natural gas storage provider. In its initial public offering presentation, the company told investors it offered predictable and growing earnings.

On June 18, 2026, short seller DF Research, also known as Dalrymple Finance, published a report on the company and said it held a position in the shares. DF Research reviewed Rockpoint's financial filings and the history of its core assets, which were previously public as Niska Gas Storage before collapsing.

The report alleged that Rockpoint is a cyclical business dependent on natural gas spreads rather than a stable growth company. It said the dollar volume of the company's sales backlog was down about 37% year over year and alleged that sponsor Brookfield Asset Management had pulled roughly $2.7 billion out of Rockpoint since its initial public offering.
Rockpoint's shares shrugged off the report and finished higher.

title: A 4.6 MB worm file slipped past GitHub code search across 3,000 repositories
points: Starting on June 10, 2026, Deep Specter Research investigated a supply-chain worm called Shai-Hulud using only public data and static-only methods.
The report said the worm used stolen maintainer tokens to commit a roughly 4.6 MB obfuscated file into trusted repositories and forged commit dates to hide the changes.
Deep Specter Research said it found 516 live malicious packages across five ecosystems, more than 3,000 affected GitHub repositories and over 200 compromised developer accounts.
body: GitHub is a software development platform that stores, displays and searches code repositories. It operates a bug disclosure channel on HackerOne where researchers can submit vulnerability reports.

Starting on June 10, 2026, Deep Specter Research investigated a supply-chain worm called Shai-Hulud using only public data and static-only methods. The report said the worm used stolen maintainer tokens to commit a roughly 4.6 MB obfuscated file into trusted repositories and forged commit dates to hide the changes.

The investigators alleged that GitHub code search ignores files that large, hiding the payload from automated scanning while five editor and tool triggers ran the code automatically. Deep Specter Research said it found 516 live malicious packages across five ecosystems, more than 3,000 affected GitHub repositories and over 200 compromised developer accounts.

On June 17, 2026, Deep Specter Research published its findings. The researchers said GitHub had rejected two formal vulnerability reports on these design flaws, closing both as ineligible and not presenting a security risk.

title: Gildan reported steady growth while $510 million in excess stock sat with distributors
points: The report alleged Gildan had stuffed distributors with about $510 million of excess product as of Q1 2026 using lengthy payment terms and a right of return.
It estimated Gildan pulled forward around $500 million in future revenue and that underlying revenue would have declined for the past three years.
Gildan shares fell 2.8% on June 16, 2026, their steepest drop in more than six years.
body: Gildan Activewear Inc. is a Canadian T-shirt and apparel manufacturer listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It told investors its revenue was growing.

On June 16, 2026, Jehoshaphat Research published a report and said it held a short position in the stock, meaning it earns when the shares fall. The firm examined Gildan's SEC filings and added back receivables Gildan had transferred off its balance sheet, finding that days sales outstanding reached nearly 200 days at the top distributor.

The report alleged Gildan had stuffed distributors with about $510 million of excess product as of Q1 2026 using lengthy payment terms and a right of return. It estimated Gildan pulled forward around $500 million in future revenue and that underlying revenue would have declined for the past three years.
Gildan shares fell 2.8% on June 16, 2026, their steepest drop in more than six years. The $510 million figure is an estimate of excess inventory held by distributors, not a loss in share value.

On November 20, 2026, law firm Kaplan Fox & Kilsheimer LLP announced a class action lawsuit had been filed on behalf of investors who bought Gildan securities between February 19, 2025, and June 15, 2026.

title: Redwire authorized $1.1 billion in share sales while losing $200 million
points: On June 12 and June 29, 2026, short seller Fugazi Research published reports examining Redwire's public filings.
The reports also cited public filings showing auditor KPMG issued an adverse opinion on Redwire's internal controls for fiscal 2025.
Redwire settled a securities class action lawsuit for $8 million over statements about its accounting practices.
body: Redwire Corporation is a space and defense contractor listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It told investors a story of rapid growth through acquisitions in space infrastructure and defense drones.

On June 12 and June 29, 2026, short seller Fugazi Research published reports examining Redwire's public filings. The investigator reviewed the company's quarterly reports and share sale programs, noting that it holds a short position and profits when the shares fall.

Fugazi Research alleged that Redwire funded acquisitions by diluting shareholders rather than generating cash. According to the reports, the company authorized $1.1 billion across three at-the-market share programs since November 2025, while trailing-twelve-month net losses reached $200 million and common shares nearly tripled in fifteen months.

The reports also cited public filings showing auditor KPMG issued an adverse opinion on Redwire's internal controls for fiscal 2025. In March 2025, Redwire settled a securities class action lawsuit for $8 million over statements about its accounting practices. Redwire's shares fell 50.13% following the report.

title: Ensign's Nursing Homes Were Allegedly Short 5,248,725 Staff Hours
points: Muddy Waters Research said it had sent investigators to 57 of Ensign's 379 facilities across eight states.
It alleged that about 20% of facilities operated without a licensed administrator supervising them, using consulting contracts to list administrators who seldom appeared.
It also cited CMS reports from 2023 and 2024 identifying unlicensed operators at four Ensign facilities.
body: The Ensign Group is a US operator of nursing facilities. It told investors it was focusing on very sick residents to increase government payments. Medicare and Medicaid accounted for 69% of its revenue.

On June 11, 2026, Muddy Waters Research said it had sent investigators to 57 of Ensign's 379 facilities across eight states. It alleged that about 20% of facilities operated without a licensed administrator supervising them, using consulting contracts to list administrators who seldom appeared. Muddy Waters held a short position, which benefits when shares fall.

Muddy Waters estimated that ending these practices would cut Ensign's 2027 operating profit, measured as EBIT, by about 35% against analyst expectations. It also cited CMS reports from 2023 and 2024 identifying unlicensed operators at four Ensign facilities.

On June 26, 2026, Hunterbrook Media published an analysis of federal staffing and cost records. It estimated that 301 Ensign facilities had a staffing gap of 5,248,725 hours, representing $161 million in estimated savings. Separately, it calculated at least $339 million in payments to related companies from 208 Ensign facilities.

Hunterbrook reported that its methods had been reviewed by three independent experts. Its affiliated investment firm held a short position in Ensign and a long position in comparable securities when the investigation was published.

title: Viceroy claimed Abaxx Exchange activity was wash-traded churn. Shares fell 13.8%.
points: Viceroy also claimed that Singapore filings showed CBOE had exited its strategic investment in Abaxx Exchange without public disclosure by the company.
Abaxx Technologies shares fell 13.8% that day.
Viceroy published another report, and on June 26, 2026, it sent a letter to the OSC and CIRO requesting an investigation.
body: Abaxx Technologies is a Canadian company that operates Abaxx Exchange.

On June 11, 2026, short seller Viceroy Research published a report and said it held a short position in Abaxx Technologies, meaning it earns when the shares fall. Viceroy alleged that Abaxx Exchange activity consisted of wash-traded churn sustained by incentives, with minimal size, wide spreads and limited depth on its central limit order book.
Viceroy also claimed that Singapore filings showed CBOE had exited its strategic investment in Abaxx Exchange without public disclosure by the company. Abaxx Technologies shares fell 13.8% that day.

On June 12, 2026, Viceroy sent a letter to MAS providing trade-level, time-stamped evidence from the previous day that it said showed artificial trading activity. On June 15, 2026, Viceroy published another report, and on June 26, 2026, it sent a letter to the OSC and CIRO requesting an investigation.

title: Five of Rwanda's Seven Largest Coltan Exporters Bought Conflict Minerals
points: Global Witness spent a year tracing coltan from Rubaya, where 15% of the world's coltan is extracted.
Investigators reviewed customs data, trade records and interviews with over 70 people, and travelled with a smuggler past M23 checkpoints.
Seven Rwandan companies exported almost 85% of the country's coltan from January 2023 to September 2025.
body: Sony is a Japanese company whose products use minerals found in smartphones and computers. Its supply chain policy requires suppliers to comply with its code of conduct. On June 10, 2026, Global Witness reported that conflict coltan from the Democratic Republic of Congo likely entered Sony's supply chain.

Global Witness spent a year tracing coltan from Rubaya, where 15% of the world's coltan is extracted. Investigators reviewed customs data, trade records and interviews with over 70 people, and travelled with a smuggler past M23 checkpoints.

The report alleged that five of Rwanda's seven biggest coltan exporters bought conflict coltan. Seven Rwandan companies exported almost 85% of the country's coltan from January 2023 to September 2025.

Four traders told investigators that smuggled coltan received ITSCI tags indicating no conflict links. Sony told Global Witness that it expects all suppliers to comply with its supply chain code of conduct and policy.
In early 2026, ITSCI told Global Witness that three additional exporters were under review and at risk of suspension and expulsion. Global Witness published its full report on June 18, 2026.

title: SEGG issued 12 press releases in 2025. A short seller said its website had one link.
points: The report alleged that 12 press releases from 2025 were fiction and that SEGG was delinquent in filing its 2025 10-K and Q126 10-Q.
SEGG said its share price dropped by more than 50% after the report came out.
SEGG sued White Diamond Research and Adam Gefvert in Tarrant County District Court in Texas for $20 million in damages.
body: Sports Entertainment Gaming Global, or SEGG Media, is a Nasdaq-listed company that told investors about deals in sports media, lotteries and prediction markets. It published press releases announcing acquisitions, international expansion and a Polymarket deal.

On June 10, 2026, short seller White Diamond Research published a report saying it may hold a short position, meaning it earns when the shares fall. It checked SEGG's corporate website and found a single webpage with no links except to an investor page.

The report alleged that 12 press releases from 2025 were fiction and that SEGG was delinquent in filing its 2025 10-K and Q126 10-Q. It also asserted that the Sports.com platform had not materialized.
SEGG said its share price dropped by more than 50% after the report came out. The company denied the claims, calling them false, misleading and disparaging.

On June 26, 2026, SEGG sued White Diamond Research and Adam Gefvert in Tarrant County District Court in Texas for $20 million in damages. SEGG also announced the launch of prediction market contracts for FIFA World Cup matches through Sports Predicts.

title: China Yuchai reported 66% earnings growth. A short seller questioned its data center engines.
points: J Capital noted that the broader Chinese truck market grew by no more than 1.5% in 2025 excluding new energy vehicles.
China Yuchai shares fell 6.2% on June 10, 2026.
The report also noted that Chinese authorities had detained the Guangxi Yuchai Machinery president and corporate chief accountant in October 2025.
body: China Yuchai International is an engine maker that reported 66% earnings growth and about 30% revenue growth in 2025. The company also touted growth in high-powered engines used for data center cooling.

On June 10, 2026, short seller J Capital Research published a report questioning whether that growth could last. J Capital noted that the broader Chinese truck market grew by no more than 1.5% in 2025 excluding new energy vehicles.

The report alleged that China Yuchai only produced a small portion of its data center engines itself and bought the rest outside for resale. It also pointed to financial statement items suggesting the company could be booking sales that might not get paid without special bank financing.
China Yuchai shares fell 6.2% on June 10, 2026. The report also noted that Chinese authorities had detained the Guangxi Yuchai Machinery president and corporate chief accountant in October 2025.

title: Azure Holding Group booked $14.3 million in inventory from a partner with $48,000 in cash
points: According to the report, CTT held $48,000 in cash, had negative cash flow, and had no revenue growth.
AZRH shares collapsed from $2.40 to $0.06.
The collapse in the share price and the booked inventory are separate figures: the stock fell from $2.40 to $0.06, while the $14.3 million was an alleged accounting entry.
body: Azure Holding Group Corp. traded over the counter under the ticker AZRH and told investors it operated oil wells in the Permian Basin across Ector, Crane, and Pecos Counties in West Texas.

On June 7, 2026, Nick Nemeth published a report at Mispriced Assets alleging that CEO Josh Cohen booked $14.3 million of inventory from a joint-venture partner, CTT. According to the report, CTT held $48,000 in cash, had negative cash flow, and had no revenue growth.
Nemeth also reported that Freedom Well Testing was bought for stock in November 2024 and sold back to its original owner for $1 in June 2025, leaving behind $1.8 million of undisclosed vendor debt.
On March 28, 2026, Cohen had posted publicly that he was broke after merchant cash advances came due. AZRH shares collapsed from $2.40 to $0.06.

Cohen was arrested on two Texas first-degree felonies. The collapse in the share price and the booked inventory are separate figures: the stock fell from $2.40 to $0.06, while the $14.3 million was an alleged accounting entry.

title: A short seller called CitroTech's fire retardant a three-decade-old product

Eleven days later, CitroTech was named a B2i Digital Featured Company to broaden its shareholder base.

title: Short seller says Formula 1 tire maker Pirelli hides Russia profits
points: The firm based its report on generally available information, field research, and Russian-language documents it translated.
Grizzly Research alleged that Pirelli depends on Russia for a far larger share of its profits than investors understand.

body: Pirelli & C. S.p.A. is a €6.7 billion Italian tire maker listed on Borsa Italiana. It is Formula 1's exclusive tire supplier.

On June 4, 2026, Grizzly Research published a short report on the company and went short the stock, meaning it earns when the shares fall. The firm based its report on generally available information, field research, and Russian-language documents it translated.

title: Alpha School charged $65,000 a year for a campus that was not a school
points: The statement had 13 named signatories and 22 additional supporters who withheld their names.
After WIRED began contacting employees in April 2026, Alpha resubmitted its application for incorporation as a school.
The June 4 investigation also described a Miami fire inspection in October 2025 that found students occupying areas not yet approved for use.
body: Alpha School is a US network of private learning centers that uses learning apps and classroom guides. In fall 2025, its executives pitched a new Manhattan campus to wealthy New York City parents. The annual cost was $65,000.

On June 4, 2026, WIRED published an investigation based on interviews with people involved in opening Alpha campuses and previously unreported documents. It obtained a New York State Education Department decision showing that the state had declined Alpha's application to incorporate as an independent school the previous summer.

People familiar with the Manhattan campus questioned whether parents understood that their children would attend a homeschooling support center rather than a school. A group of parents responded with a statement saying they knew the distinction. The statement had 13 named signatories and 22 additional supporters who withheld their names.

Alpha said every participating parent knew the New York location was a homeschooling learning center, not a school. It also said its facilities complied with applicable laws. WIRED found an internal document that placed opening dates ahead of safety and operability.

After WIRED began contacting employees in April 2026, Alpha resubmitted its application for incorporation as a school. The June 4 investigation also described a Miami fire inspection in October 2025 that found students occupying areas not yet approved for use.

title: Astrotech pivoted five times and ran up a $262 million deficit
points: Short seller Fugazi Research published a report examining Astrotech's May 14, 2026 quarterly filing for the period ended March 31, 2026.
Fugazi Research also alleged that the chief executive's son-in-law received $211,000 in software consulting fees over nine months, equal to nearly 30% of company revenue for that period.
